title: Drone Panorama Stitching: PTGui-powered exposure control, rectilinear projection, and sky replacement

date.basis: Embedded creation time in metadata; video file indicates a 2024-2025 release window.

summary: This video demonstrates a drone panorama workflow that avoids automatic exposure merging by Lightroom, instead manually balancing exposure across frame imports, then stitching with PTGui using rectilinear projection for a faithful wide-angle look. It covers cropping to a center region, and a separate sky replacement technique achieved by duplicating the sky, overlaying and masking with careful edge blending, followed by post-processing to introduce directional light and color grading. The narration highlights the advantages of PTGui's exposure fusion controls and the speed advantage over Photoshop for stitching, and it provides practical tips on masking, inverse selections, and soft brush painting to achieve a high-resolution panorama (over 100 MP).

sections.title: Pre-stitch exposure management for drone panos
sections.description: Introductory notes on how drone panos differ from still-camera panos, with a focus on lack of user control over exposure across frames and the decision to avoid letting Lightroom stitch automatically; plan is to balance exposures manually before stitching.

sections.title: PTGui-based stitching workflow and projection choices
sections.description: Demonstrates moving from Lightroom/PS to PTGui for stitching, aligning frames, selecting a projection (rectilinear) to mimic wide-angle warping, and leveraging exposure fusion controls while planning a center-crop cropping.

sections.title: Sky replacement and masking strategy
sections.description: Shows a sky replacement workflow by duplicating the image, extending the sky region, overlaying and blending the skies with careful masking, and avoiding obvious seams through inverse selection and soft blending.

sections.title: Post-processing for depth and color grading
sections.description: Covers painting light onto ridges to create three-dimensionality, directional light bleed, and final color grading to achieve a cohesive, high-contrast look.
